text: Martha Rosler, born in 1943 in Brooklyn, New York, is an American conceptual artist known for her work in photography, photo-text, video, installation, sculpture, site-specific and performance art, as well as writing on art and culture. Her work centers on everyday life and the public sphere, with a focus on women's experiences, media, war, architecture, and the built environment—including housing, homelessness, transportation, and urban planning. Rosler spent formative years in California from 1968 to 1980, first in north San Diego county and then in San Francisco, and has also lived and taught in Canada. She graduated from Erasmus Hall High School in Brooklyn, Brooklyn College in 1965, and the University of California, San Diego in 1974. She has resided in New York City since 1981. Rosler's media include photomontage and photo-text, video, sculpture, and installation. She has lectured nationally and internationally and taught photography and media, photo and video history, and critical studies at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, New Jersey, where she was a professor for thirty years and attained the rank of Professor II. She also taught at the Städelschule in Frankfurt, Germany, and served as a visiting professor at the University of California campuses in San Diego and Irvine, among other institutions. Solo exhibitions of her work have been held by the Whitney Museum of American Art (1977), Institute of Contemporary Art in Boston (1987), Museum of Modern Art in Oxford (1990), The New Museum in collaboration with the International Center of Photography in New York (1998–2000), Sprengel Hannover Museum (2005), Institute of Contemporary Arts in London (2006), University of Rennes (2006), and Portikus in Frankfurt (2008). Her work has been included in major group exhibitions such as the Whitney Biennial (1979, 1983, 1987, 1990), Documenta 7 and 12 (1982 and 2007), Havana Biennale (1986), Venice Biennale (2003), Liverpool Biennial (2004), Taipei Biennial (2004), and Skulptur Projekte (2007). She serves on advisory boards for the Whitney Museum of American Art, the Museum of Modern Art, and the Center for Urban Pedagogy in New York City, and is a board member of the Vera List Center for Art and Politics at the New School and an Advisory Board member of the Center for Urban Pedagogy. She has also served on the board of directors of the Temple Hoyne Buell Center for the Study of American Architecture at Columbia University and was a former member of the boards of the Association for Independent Video and Film and the Media Alliance, and a former trustee of the Van Alen Center, all in New York City. Since the early 1980s, she has been a regular lecturer at the Whitney Independent Study Program in New York. Rosler is known for her writing and artwork, having published over 16 books of her art and critical essays on art, photography, and cultural matters, some of which have been translated. Her essays have been widely published, anthologized, and translated, including her 1981 essay "In, Around, and Afterthoughts (on documentary photography)," which has been widely cited and credited with challenging myths of photographic disinterestedness. She was interviewed for the film !Women Art Revolution. Semiotics of the Kitchen (1974/75) is a pioneering feminist video work in which Rosler parodies early television cooking shows by demonstrating kitchen tools in alphabetical order, with gestures that shift into unexpected and alarming actions, using her body as a semaphore system. She suggests the work challenges social expectations of women in food production and the role of language in shaping those expectations, raising the question of whether women can "speak themselves." The work is seen as pioneering not because of its high production quality, but because of its low quality, which gave it a naïf, raw appearance. Other video works include Vital Statistics of a Citizen, Simply Obtained (1977), Losing: A Conversation with the Parents (1977), Martha Rosler Reads Vogue (1982), Domination and the Everyday (1980), Born to Be Sold: Martha Rosler Reads the Strange Case of Baby $/M (1988), and Secrets From the Street: No Disclosure (1980), A Simple Case for Torture, or How to Sleep at Night (1983), If It's Too Bad to be True, It Could Be DISINFORMATION (1985), Global Taste: A Meal in Three Courses (1985), and Because This Is Britain (2014). Rosler uses performance-based narratives and symbolic images from mass media to disrupt viewer expectations, stating that "video itself 'isn't innocent:' Yet video lets me construct, using a variety of fictional narrative forms, 'decoys' engaged in a dialectic with commercial TV." Her photo/text work The Bowery in two inadequate descriptive systems (1974/75) is a seminal piece in conceptual and postmodern photography, featuring 45 black and white prints that pair photos of Bowery storefronts with metaphoric texts about drunken behavior, displayed in a grid to highlight the limitations of visual and linguistic systems in describing social issues. Her best-known series, House Beautiful: Bringing the War Home (c. 1967–72), consists of photomontages that juxtapose aspirational middle-class home interiors with documentary images from the Vietnam War, originally distributed as photocopied fliers and in underground newspapers. These works draw on the traditions of John Heartfield, Hannah Höch, and Richard Hamilton, linking the industries of war and domestic life. Rosler revisited this series in 2004 and 2008 with new images based on the Iraq and Afghanistan wars, titled House Beautiful: Bringing the War Home, New Series, to address continuities with the Vietnam era and unsettle complacent viewers, noting the "rah rah" attitude of American media and politics reminiscent of past political manipulation. Her earlier series, Body Beautiful, or Beauty Knows No Pain (c. 1965–72), addresses the representation of women and domesticity and preceded the antiwar montages. Many of her works explore geopolitics of entitlement and dispossession, including series on roads, air transport, and urban undergrounds. Her art frequently integrates antiwar and feminist ideologies from the 1960s and 2000s, inserting domestic themes into the public sphere to make political, social, and instructional critiques. Rosler has had numerous solo exhibitions, including a retrospective “Positions in the Life World” (1998–2000) shown in five European cities (Birmingham, Vienna, Lyon/Villeurbanne, Barcelona, Rotterdam) and concurrently at the International Center of Photography and the New Museum of Contemporary Art in New York. A major retrospective was held at the Galleria Civica d’Arte Moderna e Contemporanea (GAM) in Turin. In 2006, her work was exhibited at the University of Rennes and in 2007 at the Worcester Museum of Art. Her work has been featured in the Venice Biennale (2003), Liverpool Biennial, Taipei Biennial (2004), Singapore Biennale (2011), and Thessaloniki Biennale (2017), as well as major international surveys including Documenta (1982, 2007), Skulptur Projekte Münster (2007), and multiple Whitney Biennials. In 1989, in lieu of a solo exhibition at the Dia Art Foundation, Rosler organized "If You Lived Here...", a project involving over 50 artists, film and video producers, photographers, architects, planners, homeless people, squatters, activist groups, and schoolchildren, addressing contested living situations, architecture, and utopian visions through three exhibitions, four public forums, and associated events. In 2009, an archive exhibition, "If You Lived Here Still," opened at e-flux in New York and traveled to Casco Office for Art Design and Theory in Utrecht and La Virreina Centre de la Imatge in Barcelona. Following this, Rosler and urbanist Miguel Robles-Durán developed an urban installation project in Hamburg, Germany, called We Promise! (2015), which critiques the conflicting promises of urban regeneration through public posters. Versions of the 1989 show have been mounted in many locations worldwide. In 2016, a planned year-long project at the New Foundation Seattle, under the title "Housing Is a Human Right," was intended to reprise the three exhibitions of "If You Lived Here..." with a focus on contemporary Seattle, but the foundation ceased operations after completing the first two shows. In response, Rosler organized an exhibition in New York in 2016, titled If you can't afford to live here, mo-o-ove!, at Mitchell-Innes and Nash, renamed as the Temporary Office of Urban Disturbances, which included material from the Dia and Seattle projects and focused on New York City, with public forums on art, gentrification, and housing privatization. At the Utopia Station exhibition at the Venice Biennale in 2003, Rosler collaborated with about 30 students from Stockholm and Copenhagen, a group called 'the Fleas,' and her graduate students from Yale to produce a mini-pavilion left unfinished, large banners, a collective newspaper, and various projects exploring utopian communities and their social and political implications. She has also produced two historical site tours—one in Hamburg (1993) and one in Liverpool (2004)—in conjunction with curated art projects. At the Frieze Art Fair in London (2005), she conducted a tour of the temporary site, covering its construction, labor, customer service, food service, toilets, VIP lounges, publicity, maintenance, and security. Her solo show Meta-Monumental Garage Sale was held at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York in November 2012, revisiting exhibitions from 1973 in San Diego and 1977 in San Francisco centered on American garage sales. The 2012 MoMA event, held in the atrium, was inspired by her interest in garage sales as a social form of small-scale, local commerce largely organized by women, which she encountered when moving to Southern California. At the request of curators, she restaged such sales in European art locales and New York City beginning in 1999, culminating in the Fair Trade Garage Sale at the Museum of Cultural History in Basel (2010) and the MoMA 2012 event. The 2012 sale offered over 14,000 items, including Rosler’s accumulated holdings and items collected from museum employees and the public, with two issues of a newspaper and two public discussions, one of which included a psychic assessing value and meaning. The work, initiated in 1973, aims to provoke questions about art and value by being held in museum or gallery spaces and to highlight the liminal domestic spaces women navigate economically. Starting in November 2005, e-flux sponsored the "Martha Rosler Library," a reading room offering over 7,500 volumes from her private collection as a public resource in venues such as art institutions, schools, and libraries. The collection began at e-flux in New York and traveled to the Frankfurter Kunstverein, Antwerp’s NICC (with MuHKA), United Nations Plaza School in Berlin, Institut National de L'Histoire de L'Art in Paris, Stills in Edinburgh, John Moore's Art School in Liverpool, and the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, before being retired. Visitors could sit and read or make free photocopies, with local reading groups and public readings organized. In 2018, the Jewish Museum in New York presented Martha Rosler: Irrespective, a survey exhibition showcasing her five decades-long practice, featuring installations, photographic series, sculpture, and video from the 1960s to the present. While her Dia exhibition aimed to expose the invisibility of homelessness and urban policies that conceal the socially underprivileged, one critique was that it did little to alleviate the homelessness problem in America. When asked about activism as an artist versus as a practitioner, Rosler stated that being an activist requires intensive work with specific communities and issues, outcomes, and that she is an artist and professor; activism is an ongoing process, and while she worked with activists on the project, she emphasized that activists do not expect intractable problems to be solved by exhibitions or campaigns in six months. Rosler is known for addressing a wide range of social and political issues, including civil rights, anti-war efforts, and women's rights. Her son, Josh Neufeld, is a graphic novelist, and the two have collaborated on several projects. Her essays have been published in catalogues, magazines such as Artforum, Afterimage, Quaderns, and Grey Room, and in edited collections including Women Artists at the Millennium (October Books/MIT, 2006). She has produced numerous "word works" and photo/text publications, including mock dialogues between Julia Child and Craig Claiborne, analyses of women in Russia, and responses to repression, crisis, and war.

Martha Rosler is an artist and professor known for creating activist and political work, often engaging with issues such as anti-war efforts and women's rights. She frequently collaborates with her students, fostering a new generation of political artists with diverse backgrounds. Rosler's son is the graphic novelist Josh Neufeld, with whom she has worked on several projects. Her essays have been widely published in magazines like Artforum, Afterimage, Quaderns, and Grey Room, as well as in edited collections such as Women Artists at the Millennium (October Books/MIT, 2006). She has produced many "word works" and photo/text publications, currently exploring themes like cookery through a mock dialogue between Julia Child and Craig Claiborne, imagery of women in Russia, and responses to repression, crisis, and war. Her 1981 essay, "In, Around, and Afterthoughts (on documentary photography)," has been widely cited, republished, and translated, playing a key role in challenging the myth of photographic disinterestedness and highlighting the influence of institutional and discursive framing on photographic meaning. Rosler has published sixteen books on photography, art, and writing, including Decoys and Disruptions: Selected Essays 1975-2001 (MIT Press, 2004), Passionate Signals (Cantz, 2005), In the Place of the Public: Observations of a Frequent Flyer (Cantz, 1997), and Rights of Passage (NYFA, 1995). If You Lived Here (Free Press, 1991) complements her Dia project on housing, homelessness, and urban life. In 2006, several books in English and other languages were released, including a 25-year edition of 3 Works (Press of the Nova Scotia College of Art and Design) with a new foreword by Rosler. The Spanish collection Imágenes Públicas, containing translations of essays and video scripts, was published in 2007. Her book Culture Class, addressing gentrification, artists, art institutions, and the Culture Class theory, was published by e-flux and Sternberg Press in 2013.
